question: Niko controls [Metallurgeon] and [Ornithopter of Paradise]. Avery casts [Prismari Command], choosing the "deal 2 damage" and "destroy target artifact" modes, targeting Ornithopter of Paradise with both. In response, Niko activates Metallurgeon's ability targeting Ornithopter of Paradise. What happens?
answer:
Ornithopter of Paradise survives, tapped, with no damage marked on it. Niko's Metallurgeon ability resolves first (it was activated later, so it's on top of the stack) and creates a regeneration shield on Ornithopter of Paradise. A regeneration effect is a replacement effect that replaces a destruction event: instead of being destroyed, the permanent is tapped, all damage marked on it is removed, and it's removed from combat [701.8c].

Then Prismari Command resolves, following its instructions in the order written [608.2c]. The order printed on Prismari Command puts the damage mode ahead of the destroy mode, so first Ornithopter of Paradise (a 0/2) is dealt 2 damage, then the "Destroy target artifact" mode tries to destroy it. Both targets are still legal, so Prismari Command does as much as it can [Prismari Command ruling #0]. That destruction is replaced by the regeneration shield: Ornithopter of Paradise becomes tapped and the 2 damage marked on it is removed. Because no state-based check for lethal damage happens in the middle of a spell's resolution, once Prismari Command finishes resolving there is no marked damage left, so Ornithopter of Paradise is not destroyed at all. It stays on the battlefield tapped (and its mana ability can't be activated again until it's untapped).

Timing caveat: this assumes the damage mode is applied before the destroy mode, which is how Prismari Command's printed mode order works. If instead the destroy portion were somehow applied first, the shield would be spent on that destruction (tapping it, no damage to remove), and the 2 damage dealt afterward would be lethal to a 0/2, so Ornithopter of Paradise would be destroyed by state-based actions with no shield left.

Note also that Metallurgeon's ability says "Regenerate target artifact," and Ornithopter of Paradise is an artifact creature, so it's a legal target; being an artifact creature doesn't change how it interacts with artifact-targeting effects [Metallurgeon ruling #0]. Nothing here depends on the number of players — the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ahmed controls [Bronze Sable]. They cast [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Solemnity] onto the battlefield. Does Bronze Sable get a phylactery counter?
answer:
No — Bronze Sable does not get a phylactery counter, and Ahmed must then sacrifice Phylactery Lich.

Why: Genesis Wave puts Phylactery Lich and Solemnity onto the battlefield at the same time [Genesis Wave ruling #5]. Solemnity reads "Counters can't be put on artifacts, creatures, enchantments, or lands," and that stops counters from being put on such a permanent both as it enters and later [Solemnity ruling #8]. There is one narrow exception: if an artifact, creature, enchantment, or land would *enter the battlefield* with counters at the same time Solemnity enters, Solemnity doesn't stop those counters [Solemnity ruling #6]. Bronze Sable is not entering the battlefield here — it was already on the battlefield — so that exception doesn't apply, and Solemnity's static ability (functioning from the battlefield, per [113.6i]) prevents the phylactery counter. Note that "putting counters on an object" covers both counters placed on a permanent already on the battlefield and counters given as it enters [122.6a].

Separately, Phylactery Lich's own replacement instruction ("As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control") also could not have targeted a simultaneously-entering artifact anyway [Phylactery Lich ruling #1] — but that's moot since Bronze Sable was already there.

Result: Ahmed controls no permanent with a phylactery counter, so Phylactery Lich's last ability — a state trigger — triggers immediately and Ahmed sacrifices Phylactery Lich [Phylactery Lich ruling #0], [Phylactery Lich ruling #2].

If instead Solemnity had already been on the battlefield before Genesis Wave resolved, the answer is the same: no counter, sacrifice the Lich. Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents.

Abilities of all other objects usually function only while that object is on the battlefield. The exceptions are as follows: An object’s ability that states counters can’t be put on that object functions as that object is entering the battlefield in addition to functioning while that object is on the battlefield.

This refers to putting counters on that object while it’s on the battlefield and also to an object that’s given counters as it enters the battlefield. If the effect doesn’t specify a player, the object’s controller puts those counters on it.

answer_gold: Yes. Phylactery Lich and Solemnity enter the battlefield at the same time. Solemnity's effect must exist before Phylactery Lich enters the battlefield in order to prevent Bronze Sable from getting a counter.

question: Ashley controls [Tatterkite]. Ashley casts [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Humility] onto the battlefield. Can they put a phylactery counter on Tatterkite?
answer:
Yes — with Humility on the battlefield, Tatterkite is a legal choice for Phylactery Lich's counter, because Humility strips Tatterkite's "This creature can't have counters put on it" ability.

Why:

1. Humility reads "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Ability-removing effects are applied in layer 6 of the layer system [613.1f], and Tatterkite is a creature, so it loses its "can't have counters put on it" ability. Once that ability is gone, nothing stops counters from being placed on Tatterkite. Note that this is not a "can't" effect beating an "allows" effect — rule 101.2a explicitly says adding and removing abilities don't fall under that rule, and Tatterkite's text is an ordinary ability that can be removed (it isn't a "can't have [ability]" effect of the kind described in 113.11).

2. Tatterkite is still an Artifact Creature — Humility only removes abilities and sets base power/toughness to 1/1; it doesn't change card types. So Tatterkite is "an artifact you control" and thus a legal choice for Phylactery Lich's "As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control." It's already on the battlefield rather than entering alongside Phylactery Lich, so Phylactery Lich ruling #1 (you can't choose an artifact entering simultaneously) doesn't exclude it. The choice isn't a target, and no player can act between the choice and the counter being placed [Phylactery Lich ruling #3].

Timing/ambiguity I'm assuming: Genesis Wave puts Phylactery Lich and Humility onto the battlefield at the same time [Genesis Wave ruling #5], so Humility's continuous ability-removing effect is already applying when Phylactery Lich's as-enters ability is carried out. If instead Humility were not yet on the battlefield when Phylactery Lich entered (e.g., you put only Phylactery Lich in), Tatterkite would still have its ability and could not receive the counter — Phylactery Lich's ability would simply do nothing to it [Tatterkite ruling #1, Tatterkite ruling #2], and if you controlled no other permanent with a phylactery counter, Phylactery Lich's state trigger would make you sacrifice it [Phylactery Lich ruling #0, Phylactery Lich ruling #2].

One caveat the provided rules don't settle: whether Phylactery Lich's own "As this creature enters" ability still functions at all when Humility is entering simultaneously and removing its abilities. The context doesn't include a rule on when a permanent's as-enters ability is locked in relative to a simultaneously entering Humility, so I can't resolve that point from what's given. If that ability doesn't function, no counter is placed anywhere and Phylactery Lich's sacrifice trigger applies unless you control another permanent with a phylactery counter [Phylactery Lich ruling #4].

Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: Avery controls [The One Ring] and casts [Teferi's Protection] then casts a second The One Ring. What happens at the start of the next turn?
answer:
Direct answer: Assuming the next turn is Avery's turn, at the start of it (as Avery's untap step begins) the first The One Ring phases back in with its burden counters intact, and both protection-from-everything effects and the "life total can't change" effect from Teferi's Protection end (they last "until your next turn"). Avery then has two copies of the legendary The One Ring on the battlefield at once, and the upkeep trigger of each The One Ring that's on the battlefield at that time triggers, making Avery lose 1 life per burden counter on it.

Details and reasoning:

- Phasing means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist: it can't be targeted, its static abilities do nothing, its triggered abilities can't trigger, and it can't attack or block [Teferi's Protection ruling #5]. So while the first The One Ring is phased out, its upkeep ability can't trigger and it isn't "there" for anything.
- Teferi's Protection phased out only permanents Avery controlled as it resolved. The second The One Ring, cast afterward, entered the battlefield normally and is not phased out. Because it was cast, its enters trigger gave Avery protection from everything until Avery's next turn; multiple instances of protection from the same quality are redundant [702.16m].
- Phased-out permanents phase in as Avery's untap step begins, keeping their counters [Teferi's Protection ruling #15] and any choices made as they entered [Teferi's Protection ruling #24]. If Avery's untap step is skipped, the first The One Ring stays phased out until Avery's next actual untap step, but the protection and the life-total lock still end when Avery's next turn begins [Teferi's Protection ruling #21].
- Timing note on "the next turn": if the next turn belongs to another player (a real possibility in a multiplayer game, and also the case in two-player play if Avery cast these on an opponent's turn), nothing phases in on that turn — the first The One Ring stays phased out and Avery still has protection from everything until Avery's own next turn begins, at which point the phase-in and the end of protection happen.
- What I can't confirm from the provided rules: the legend rule (two legendary permanents with the same name under one controller) is not among the rules given here — the context only includes the "world rule" [704.5k] and the Role state-based action [704.5y]. So I can't state from this context how the duplicate-legendary situation is resolved once both copies of The One Ring are on the battlefield simultaneously; you'd need rule 704.5j for that.

question: Amaya controls [Dralnu, Lich Lord], [Furnace of Rath] and six [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico casts [Incinerate] targeting Dralnu, Lich Lord. If Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath, how many other permanents will they need to sacrifice?
answer:
Five other permanents (six total, one of which is Furnace of Rath) — assuming Amaya applies Furnace of Rath's doubling effect first.

How it works: Incinerate would deal 3 damage to Dralnu, Lich Lord. Two replacement effects want to apply to that damage event: Furnace of Rath ("deals double that damage") and Dralnu, Lich Lord's own "If damage would be dealt to Dralnu, sacrifice that many permanents instead." When multiple effects modify how damage would be dealt, the affected object's controller — Amaya — chooses the order (Furnace of Rath ruling #4).

- Order chosen in the question (Furnace of Rath first): 3 damage becomes 6, then Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect replaces that damage with sacrificing 6 permanents. Sacrificing Furnace of Rath counts as one of the six, so 5 other permanents must also be sacrificed. Amaya has enough (Dralnu, Lich Lord itself plus six Snow-Covered Forests remain available), and Dralnu, Lich Lord may itself be one of the sacrificed permanents (Dralnu, Lich Lord ruling #4). Note that sacrificing Furnace of Rath as part of this replacement does not un-double the damage — the doubling was already applied.
- If Amaya instead applies Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect first: only 3 permanents are sacrificed, and no damage is ever dealt, so Furnace of Rath never doubles anything — that would be 2 other permanents besides Furnace of Rath.

To sacrifice a permanent is to move it from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard; it is not destroyed, so regeneration-style effects can't apply ([701.21a]), and Incinerate's no-regeneration clause is moot since no damage is dealt at all. Also, if Dralnu, Lich Lord would be dealt more damage than the number of permanents Amaya controls, they'd simply sacrifice all of them (Dralnu, Lich Lord ruling #13) — not an issue here with eight permanents.

This answer is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table; only Nico's Incinerate and Amaya's permanents are involved.

Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.

Two or five, Amaya's choice.

Both Dralnu, Lich Lord and Furnace of Rath have replacement effects that modify how the game handles damage that is being dealt to Dralnu, Lich Lord. As Amaya is the controller of the affected object, Amaya will choose which order to apply the replacement effects in. If Amaya chooses to apply Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect first, the 3 damage will be converted into sacrificing three permanents, and Furnace of Rath will no longer apply to that event since there's no longer any damage being dealt. If they chooses to apply Furnace of Rath first, then the three damage will be doubled to six damage, and then will be replaced by sacrificing six permanents.

Whether Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath or not is irrelevant, as all replacement effects are applied to the event before anything is actually sacrificed.

question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
answer:
No — Coral Commando stops attacking. A change of a permanent's controller removes it from combat: rule 506.4a lists "if its controller changes" among the events that remove a permanent from combat, and a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature. So when Flash Conscription resolves and Arely gains control of Coral Commando until end of turn, Coral Commando is immediately removed from combat, is untapped and hasty, and deals no combat damage in the combat damage step of that combat.

Assumed timing: Flash Conscription resolves after attackers were already declared (as stated). If it had somehow resolved before the declare attackers step, Coral Commando simply wouldn't be declared as an attacker by Aubrey at all, since Arely would control it.

A couple of details worth noting:
- Gaining control after the declaration doesn't "undo" the attack event. Aubrey still declared Coral Commando as an attacker, so Aubrey has "attacked" that player for the purposes of triggers and effects that look back at the declaration (508.6), and any declare-attackers triggers (508.3) already triggered.
- Flash Conscription does not put Coral Commando back into combat on Arely's side; nothing in its text states Coral Commando is attacking, so rule 508.4/508.4b (effects that state a creature is attacking) doesn't apply, and Arely gets no combat damage or life gain from it this combat.
- In Two-Headed Giant (shared team turns), the attacking team makes one combined attack and announces what each creature is attacking (805.10b). If Arely is on the opposing team, control passes across teams and Coral Commando leaves combat as described. If Arely is Aubrey's teammate, the controller still changes from Aubrey to Arely, so rule 506.4a still removes Coral Commando from combat — being on the same team does not prevent that.

Even though Aubrey and Arely are on the same team and are both allowed to be attacking with creatures, they are different players and therefore Arely gaining control of Aubrey's creature still qualifies as a control change.

question: Nicolas controls [Razorfield Thresher], [Lake of the Dead], and [Veinfire Borderpost]. Aubrey controls [Omniscience] and casts [Casualties of War], choosing Razorfield Thresher as the artifact target and the creature target. Then they cast [Radiate], targeting Casualties of War. What will be destroyed after all spells and abilities have resolved?
answer:
Only Razorfield Thresher is destroyed.

Why: Aubrey's Casualties of War has two modes chosen — "Destroy target artifact" and "Destroy target creature" — and both instances of "target" were pointed at the same permanent, Razorfield Thresher. Because every target of Casualties of War is that one permanent, it does count as a spell that "targets only a single permanent or player," so Radiate can legally target it ([Radiate], [Casualties of War ruling #0]).

Radiate then copies Casualties of War "for each other permanent or player the spell could target," with each copy targeting a different one of those objects. To be a legal object for a copy, that single permanent has to be a legal target for *both* chosen modes at once — i.e., it must be both an artifact and a creature. Looking at the board: Lake of the Dead is a land (neither artifact nor creature), Veinfire Borderpost is an artifact but not a creature, and Aubrey's Omniscience is an enchantment. No other permanent (and no player, since neither mode targets players) can satisfy both instances of "target," so Radiate makes zero copies. Radiate itself resolves and does nothing further.

Casualties of War then resolves and destroys Razorfield Thresher in the order the modes are listed (artifact, then creature); the second instance simply has nothing left to do, but the spell still resolves normally because it has at least one legal target ([608.2b], [Casualties of War ruling #1]). Any death/leaves-the-battlefield triggers from Razorfield Thresher go on the stack only after Casualties of War finishes resolving ([Casualties of War ruling #1], [603.10a]).

Omniscience only let Aubrey cast the spells without paying mana costs; it doesn't change targeting ([Omniscience ruling #1]).

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, the answer changes only if some other player controls a permanent that is simultaneously an artifact and a creature — each such permanent would get its own Radiate copy and be destroyed too. In this two-player situation, nothing extra is destroyed.

question: Alonso controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Alonso would like to have Clone copy Spark Double, then they would like to apply the replacement effect Clone inherited from Spark Double and have it copy Spark Double again. If Alonso has Clone copy Spark Double a total of four times, how many +1/+1 counters will Clone enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Clone enters the battlefield with exactly one +1/+1 counter, no matter how many times Alonso chains the copying.

Why: Clone's own ability ("You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield") has no counter exception, so the first copy of Spark Double contributes nothing. Now Clone has Spark Double's copy ability, whose exception is "it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it's a creature." Rule 707.9e states that this kind of exception is an additional effect, not a modification of copiable characteristics, and that if another copy effect is applied to the object after applying the copy effect with the exception, the earlier exception's effect doesn't happen. So each time Alonso applies a further copy of Spark Double, the previously earned counter is wiped out. Only the last copy application's exception actually happens, giving one +1/+1 counter (Clone is a creature at that point, per Spark Double ruling #4's instruction to use Clone's characteristics as it enters). Spark Double ruling #3 confirms a creature copy enters with one +1/+1 counter plus any counters from abilities it copied — and here the only such ability is the one whose exception was superseded.

Assumption on ordering: I'm reading "four times" as four successive applications of the copy replacement effect as Clone enters, all in the same enters-the-battlefield event (rule 616.1g allows nested replacement effects to be chosen in sequence). If instead Alonso stopped after a single application of Spark Double's ability with no later copy effect, that lone exception would still yield one counter — the total is one either way.

Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, and the provided rules give no multiplayer variation for it.

question: Nickolas controls a [Nyx Herald] enchanted by [Drake Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Fracturing Gust]. How much life do they gain?
answer:
Ainsley gains 2 life (assuming Nyx Herald and Drake Umbra are the only artifacts/enchantments on the battlefield).

Why: Fracturing Gust tries to destroy all artifacts and enchantments, which includes both Drake Umbra (an enchantment Aura) and Nyx Herald (an enchantment creature). Drake Umbra's umbra armor says that if the enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy the Aura. Because Fracturing Gust would destroy both Drake Umbra and Nyx Herald simultaneously, umbra armor saves Nyx Herald, and Fracturing Gust ends up destroying Drake Umbra in two ways at once — with the same result as destroying it once [Drake Umbra ruling #4]. Umbra armor's replacement is mandatory [Drake Umbra ruling #1].

So exactly one permanent, Drake Umbra, is actually destroyed by Fracturing Gust. Nyx Herald stays on the battlefield, and Fracturing Gust gives no life for a permanent that remains on the battlefield [Fracturing Gust ruling #0]. At 2 life per permanent destroyed, that's 2 life, and Ainsley's life total is adjusted upward accordingly [119.3].

Count any other artifacts or enchantments on the battlefield (any player's) at 2 life each on top of that. This works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game; in a Two-Headed Giant game the life gain happens to Ainsley individually but is applied to Ainsley's team's shared life total [810.9].

question: Avery controls [Corpsejack Menace] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Corpsejack Menace to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield with just one +1/+1 counter, not two.

Why: Rescuer Sphinx's own text is a replacement effect applied as it enters — "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it." Returning Corpsejack Menace to Avery's hand happens as part of applying that effect, and no player takes any actions between the choice and Rescuer Sphinx being on the battlefield with its counter [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #2]. Because Corpsejack Menace has already left the battlefield by the time counters are actually placed on Rescuer Sphinx, its doubling effect ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, twice that many +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") isn't there to apply, so the single counter isn't doubled.

Corpsejack Menace can double counters a creature enters with [Corpsejack Menace ruling #0] — so if Avery had instead returned some other nonland permanent and left Corpsejack Menace on the battlefield, Rescuer Sphinx would have entered with two +1/+1 counters (and four if two Corpsejack Menaces were out, per [Corpsejack Menace ruling #1]). Also note the only legal targets to return are permanents already on the battlefield [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #0], and any "when Rescuer Sphinx enters" trigger on the returned permanent won't trigger [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #1].

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games since only Avery's own permanents are involved.

question: Arabella casts [Mind's Desire]. In response, Neil casts [Lim-Dûl's Vault]. How many copies of Mind's Desire are created when the storm trigger resolves?
answer:
Zero copies — assuming Mind's Desire was the first spell cast this turn. Neil's Lim-Dûl's Vault does not add a copy, because storm only counts spells that were cast *before* Mind's Desire this turn, and Lim-Dûl's Vault was cast afterward (in response to it).

Details:
- Storm is a triggered ability that triggers when you cast the spell: "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn" [702.40a]. So the count is spells cast earlier in the turn, by any player, regardless of what happens while the trigger is on the stack.
- More generally, the number of copies of Mind's Desire equals the number of other spells cast before Mind's Desire that turn. Spells cast from zones other than the hand and spells that were countered still count [Mind's Desire ruling #3]. So if, say, Arabella and other players had cast three spells earlier in the turn before Mind's Desire, you'd get three copies, and Lim-Dûl's Vault still wouldn't add a fourth.
- The copies are put directly onto the stack and are not cast [707.10b], [Mind's Desire ruling #4], so they also won't be counted by any later storm spell. Each copy can be countered individually; countering Mind's Desire itself doesn't remove the copies [Mind's Desire ruling #5], and Neil could instead counter the storm trigger itself to stop all copies [Mind's Desire ruling #2].

This counting works identically with two players or more than two — storm counts spells cast before it by anyone, not just by you.

question: Aubrey casts [Bitter Ordeal], targeting Natasha. At their first opportunity, Aubrey sacrifices their [Westvale Abbey]. How many cards will Aubrey be able to exile from Natasha's library?
answer:
Aubrey exiles just one card from Natasha's library — only Bitter Ordeal itself resolves; no gravestorm copies are created.

Why: gravestorm is a triggered ability that triggers when you cast Bitter Ordeal, and it counts the permanents that were put into a graveyard earlier that turn at the moment it triggers. Aubrey's first opportunity to take an action (sacrificing Westvale Abbey, or the creatures for its ability) comes after Bitter Ordeal has already been cast and the gravestorm ability has already triggered and locked in its count. Assuming nothing had already gone to a graveyard this turn, that count is zero, so zero copies are made. Anything put into a graveyard afterward is too late to matter.

Bitter Ordeal then resolves: Aubrey searches Natasha's library for a card and exiles it, and Natasha shuffles. Because Bitter Ordeal asks for a quantity of cards from a hidden zone, Aubrey must find one card if the library has at least one card, and finds nothing only if Natasha's library is empty [701.23d], [609.3]. So the total is 1 card (0 if Natasha's library is empty).

Timing note: if instead Westvale Abbey (or the five creatures for its ability) had already hit the graveyard before Bitter Ordeal was cast, gravestorm would copy Bitter Ordeal once per such permanent, and Aubrey could exile one card per copy plus one for the original. The phrase "at their first opportunity" is what puts the sacrifice too late.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since each copy simply targets a player.

question: Ainsley activates [Priest of Forgotten Gods]'s ability, but doesn't choose a target for the first part. Can Nickolas respond to the ability?
answer:
Yes. Nickolas can respond. Even with zero targets chosen, Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability uses the stack and can be responded to [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #1].

Why: the ability says "Any number of target players each lose 2 life...", so it's an ability that requires targets but permits zero to be chosen; it's simply not a targeted ability if Ainsley chooses none [115.6], and Ainsley is allowed to choose none [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #0]. Because it *may* have targets, it is not a mana ability, so it doesn't bypass the stack the way a true mana ability would (a mana ability resolves immediately and can't be targeted, countered, or responded to) [605.3b], [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #1].

So after Ainsley activates it, the ability goes on the stack and Ainsley retains priority; once players pass, Nickolas gets priority and can cast instants or activate abilities in response — for example, removing Priest of Forgotten Gods (which won't stop the ability) or countering the ability. On resolution, Ainsley still adds {B}{B} and draws a card [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #0].

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games; in a multiplayer game every other player, not just Nickolas, gets a chance to respond in turn order. Note also that if Ainsley had chosen targets, players who can't sacrifice a creature would still lose 2 life [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #2].

question: Analia controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Muldrotha, the Gravetide], and the top card of their graveyard is [Grid Monitor]. Can Analia cast the Grid Monitor?
answer:
No — Analia can't cast Grid Monitor from the graveyard while it's the top card of that graveyard.

Why: Volrath's Shapeshifter says that as long as the top card of your graveyard is a creature card, it has the full text of that card. Grid Monitor is an Artifact Creature — Construct, so it is a creature card, and Volrath's Shapeshifter therefore has Grid Monitor's text, including "You can't cast creature spells" ([Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1], [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #5]). That is a continuous prohibition in effect on the battlefield.

A player may begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows it and no rule or effect prohibits it (601.3). Legality is checked as Analia begins to cast, while Grid Monitor is still the top card of the graveyard and Volrath's Shapeshifter still carries the prohibition; continuous effects that would apply to the object are taken into account (601.3e). Muldrotha, the Gravetide grants permission to cast a permanent spell of each permanent type from your graveyard, but permission doesn't override a prohibition.

Also, you can't dodge this by "declaring" it as your artifact spell for Muldrotha, the Gravetide. A "creature spell" is any spell with the type Creature, even if it also has other types such as Artifact ([Grid Monitor ruling #1]). Grid Monitor cast from the graveyard is still a creature spell, so the prohibition applies no matter which Muldrotha, the Gravetide slot Analia announces ([Muldrotha, the Gravetide ruling #1], [Muldrotha, the Gravetide ruling #7]).

The fact that casting it would move it off the top of the graveyard (and thus turn Volrath's Shapeshifter back into a 0/1) doesn't help — the check happens before the card leaves the graveyard, and by then the cast has already been disallowed.

To cast Grid Monitor with Muldrotha, the Gravetide, Analia must first change what's on top of the graveyard (e.g., use Volrath's Shapeshifter's "{2}: Discard a card" to put a noncreature card on top... note that discarding puts the new card on top, but Grid Monitor would then no longer be the top card either, so Analia would need Grid Monitor on top only for the copy effect — practically, remove the prohibition by making the top card something other than Grid Monitor, e.g. sacrificing or bouncing Volrath's Shapeshifter, and then cast Grid Monitor from the graveyard).

This answer is the same with two players or more than two; nothing here depends on player count.

question: Antoine owns an [Eternal Scourge] that was exiled by Nico's [Ixalan's Binding]. Can Antoine cast it?
answer:
No. Antoine can't cast that Eternal Scourge — or any other card named Eternal Scourge — while Nico's Ixalan's Binding keeps it exiled.

Eternal Scourge's "You may cast this card from exile" grants permission to cast it from the exile zone, but Ixalan's Binding says "Your opponents can't cast spells with the same name as the exiled card," which is a prohibition on Antoine (an opponent of Nico). Rule 601.3 requires both that some rule or effect allow the casting and that no rule or effect prohibit it; a prohibition beats a permission, so the cast is illegal. This applies to the exiled Eternal Scourge itself and to any copy of Eternal Scourge in Antoine's hand, graveyard, etc., since Ixalan's Binding keys off the name, not the specific card. Also note Eternal Scourge's exile-cast permission doesn't waive cost or timing: Antoine would still have to pay {3} and follow normal sorcery-speed timing for a creature spell (Eternal Scourge ruling #2).

If Nico's Ixalan's Binding later leaves the battlefield, the exiled card returns to the battlefield under Antoine's control immediately (Ixalan's Binding ruling #4), and the name restriction ends.

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table: the restriction applies to all of Nico's opponents. In multiplayer, if Nico leaves the game, the exiled Eternal Scourge returns to the battlefield under Antoine's control as its owner (Ixalan's Binding ruling #1).

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
Direct answer: The resulting mutated permanent is a single face-down 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no mana cost, no creature types, and mana value 0 — the characteristics of the topmost component, the manifested card — but it has the abilities of both components, so it has Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate ability and "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token." That trigger goes off immediately from this mutation, so Avery gets a 3/3 green Beast token.

Why:
- Mutate: casting Trumpeting Gnarr for its mutate cost {3}{G/U}{G/U} makes it a mutating creature spell targeting a non-Human creature Avery owns [702.140a]. The face-down manifested permanent has no creature types at all, so it isn't a Human and is a legal target [Soul Summons ruling #8].
- As the mutating creature spell resolves with a legal target, Trumpeting Gnarr does not enter the battlefield on its own; it merges with the manifested creature, and Avery chooses top or bottom [702.140c][608.3d][730.2a].
- A mutated permanent derives its characteristics from the topmost card and has all abilities of every component [702.140e][730.2a]. Since Avery put the manifested card on top, the permanent stays a face-down 2/2 colorless nameless creature with mana value 0 [Soul Summons ruling #8], while still gaining Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities.
- "Whenever this creature mutates" triggers when a spell merges with a creature this way [702.140d], so the Beast token is created.

Later play: Avery can still turn the face-down component face up as a special action any time they have priority, by revealing it's a creature card and paying its mana cost [Soul Summons ruling #6][Soul Summons ruling #2]. If it's a noncreature card, it just stays face down [Soul Summons ruling #1]. Turning it face up doesn't retrigger enters-the-battlefield abilities [Soul Summons ruling #11].

No multiplayer wrinkle here: mutate only cares that the target is a non-Human creature with the same owner, so the answer is identical in two-player and multiplayer games [702.140a].

question: Nayeli controls a [Yixlid Jailer]. Ariel has a [Golgari Brownscale] in their graveyard and returns it to their hand with [Disturbing Plot]. Does Ariel gain 2 life?
answer:
No — Ariel does not gain 2 life.

Yixlid Jailer reads "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." Golgari Brownscale's ability, "When this card is put into your hand from your graveyard, you gain 2 life," is an ability that triggers while Golgari Brownscale is still in the graveyard (the trigger event is its leaving the graveyard for the hand). Because Yixlid Jailer strips Golgari Brownscale of all abilities while it is in the graveyard, the ability isn't there to trigger at all, so nothing goes on the stack when Disturbing Plot returns it to Ariel's hand. This is the same principle stated for abilities that trigger from the graveyard rather than from the battlefield [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4] — such abilities are stopped entirely. (By contrast, abilities that trigger on being put into a graveyard *from the battlefield* trigger from the battlefield and are unaffected [Yixlid Jailer ruling #6].)

Since no life gain event occurs, nothing that cares about life gain triggers either [119.9], and Ariel's life total is simply not adjusted [119.3].

Related notes: Golgari Brownscale's first ability normally triggers on any return to hand from the graveyard, not just via dredge [Golgari Brownscale ruling #0], but Yixlid Jailer removes it regardless. Golgari Brownscale's Dredge 2 also can't be used while Yixlid Jailer is on the battlefield, for the same reason (it's a graveyard ability). Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Yixlid Jailer affects cards in all graveyards.

question: Aryana has taken control of an [Ahn-Crop Crasher] from Noe with [Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded], which Aryana exerts. After Aryana ends their turn, will it untap during Noe's untap step?
answer:
Yes. Ahn-Crop Crasher will untap normally during Noe's untap step.

Exerting means you choose to have the permanent not untap during *your* next untap step ([701.43a]). Since Aryana gained control of Ahn-Crop Crasher only until end of turn via Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded's −6 ability, control reverts to Noe as the turn ends, and Aryana's next untap step never happens while Ahn-Crop Crasher is under Aryana's control. The exert effect therefore doesn't stop it from untapping during Noe's untap step ([Ahn-Crop Crasher ruling #4]).

During Noe's untap step, Noe (the active player) determines which of their permanents untap and untaps them all simultaneously as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack ([502.3], [703.4c]); normally everything Noe controls untaps, so Ahn-Crop Crasher untaps. No player gets priority in the untap step, so nothing can be cast or activated to change this then ([502.4]).

This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer — the relevant point is simply that the exert restriction is tied to the exerting player's own untap step, not the controller's at that later time.

Then they untap them all simultaneously. See rule 502.3.

question: Andres controls [Strionic Resonator] and plays [Clive's Hideaway]. They activate Strionic Resonator targeting the hideaway trigger, exiling 2 cards. On their next turn, they activate Clive's Hideaway's ability to cast the exiled card. What happens as it resolves?
answer:
As Clive's Hideaway's {2}, {T} ability resolves, "the exiled card" refers to both cards exiled by the Hideaway 4 trigger and by the Strionic Resonator copy, so Andres may play either or both of them without paying their mana costs — provided he controls four or more legendary creatures at that time.

Why: Hideaway 4 is a triggered ability ([702.75a]) that exiles a card face down, and Clive's Hideaway's {2}, {T} ability referring to "the exiled card" is linked to it ([607.2a]). When Strionic Resonator copies a triggered ability, the copy is linked to that same second ability, so "the exiled card" means every card exiled by the original trigger and the copy [Strionic Resonator ruling #1]. When such an ability gets multiple answers for "the exiled card," all of them apply [Strionic Resonator ruling #3] — here that means both exiled cards may be played, each without paying its mana cost, one at a time in any order as the ability resolves (a land play would still use a land play; a spell is cast during the resolution).

The "four or more legendary creatures" condition is checked as Clive's Hideaway's ability resolves; if Andres doesn't control four legendary creatures then, he plays neither card and the cards simply stay exiled (he may still look at them, per [702.75a]). Also note that if one of the exiled cards is an adventurer card, playing it this way lets him choose to cast it as an Adventure ([715.3d]).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the Strionic Resonator copy was made while the Hideaway trigger was still on the stack (the only legal window — Strionic Resonator can only target a triggered ability already on the stack, [Strionic Resonator ruling #0], [603.3c]), and that the second exile therefore came from the copy. If instead the second card had been exiled by some unlinked, separate effect, Clive's Hideaway's ability would only find the card its own linked trigger exiled ([607.2a], [607.5]).

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

If that ability asks for any information about the exiled card, such as a characteristic or mana value, it gets multiple answers. question: Aminah has no cards in their library and activate [Words of Wind] in their upkeep. Do they lose the game?
answer:
No — Aminah doesn't lose the game from that draw. Words of Wind's activated ability sets up a replacement effect for the next card Aminah would draw this turn. A draw-replacement effect is applied even if the affected player's library is empty ([121.6a]), so when Aminah's draw step draw event happens, it is replaced by "each player returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand" — no card is actually drawn from the empty library, so nothing triggers the state-based action that makes a player who attempted to draw from an empty library lose the game ([704.5b], [121.4], [104.3c]).

Assumed timing: Aminah activates Words of Wind during their upkeep step (no draw happens then), and the ability resolves before their draw step, so the replacement is available and consumes the draw step's single draw. If instead the draw had already been attempted from the empty library before the ability resolved, Aminah would lose the game the next time a player would receive priority ([121.4]).

Caution: only one draw is replaced per activation. Any further draw this turn (or the next turn's draw step) with an empty library will make Aminah lose. If Aminah activated Words of Wind multiple times, they choose which one to apply and use up on each draw ([Words of Wind ruling #0]).

Multiplayer note: the replacement effect makes each player (Aminah included) return a permanent they control to its owner's hand, so with more than two players every opponent bounces a permanent; the game-loss analysis for Aminah is identical in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Allan controls [Living Inferno]. They activate it, targeting Nathaly's [Runeclaw Bear]. In response, Nathaly casts [Chemister's Trick], targeting the Living Inferno. How much damage will be dealt to Runeclaw Bear when the Living Inferno's ability resolves?
answer:
8 damage is dealt to Nathaly's Runeclaw Bear.

Because Living Inferno's ability divides damage among targets, the amount of damage it will deal is locked in when the ability is activated — at that time Living Inferno's power was 8, so 8 damage is assigned to the single target, Runeclaw Bear [Living Inferno ruling #0][Living Inferno ruling #1]. Nathaly's Chemister's Trick makes Living Inferno an 6/5 (-2/-0 is a power-changing effect applied in layer 7 [613.1g]), but that change comes after the division was locked in and therefore does not reduce the damage dealt to Runeclaw Bear [Living Inferno ruling #1].

The second half of the ability is different: each targeted creature deals damage equal to its power to Living Inferno, and that amount is determined on resolution. Runeclaw Bear is a 2/2, so it deals 2 damage to Living Inferno, which (now 6/5) survives — 8 damage to Runeclaw Bear destroys it, but combat/ability damage is dealt simultaneously as one event, so Runeclaw Bear still deals its 2 [120.4b][120.4d].

Note also that Chemister's Trick's "attacks this turn if able" clause is irrelevant here to the ability's damage. This all works identically whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on player count.

Awe Strike’s effect is applied, so the damage event becomes [5 damage is dealt to the defending player, the defending player gains 5 life]. That’s processed into its results, so the damage event is now [the defending player loses 5 life, the defending player gains 5 life]. Worship’s effect sees that the damage event would not reduce the player’s life total to less than 1, so Worship’s effect is not applied. Then the damage event occurs.

question: After both players finish taking mulligans, Adrian is going second and has both [Gemstone Caverns] and [Chancellor of the Annex] in their hand. Can they reveal Chancellor of the Annex for its ability and also exile it to begin the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield?
answer:
Yes — Adrian can do both, revealing Chancellor of the Annex and then exiling that same Chancellor of the Annex as the cost of starting the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield.

Why: Both cards grant actions taken from the opening hand (the hand you have after all mulligans are finished). Because Adrian is not the starting player, the starting player takes all of their opening-hand actions first, then Adrian may take any and all of theirs in any order ([103.6], [103.6a], [103.6b], [Gemstone Caverns ruling #0], [Chancellor of the Annex ruling #2]). Adrian is not limited to one such action.

Order matters for what you get:
- Reveal Chancellor of the Annex first. Revealing does not move a card out of the zone it's in, so Chancellor of the Annex is still in hand afterward ([701.20b]). The reveal sets up its delayed trigger: when each opponent casts their first spell of the game, that spell is countered unless they pay {1} (that's {1} generic, payable with any mana).
- Then take Gemstone Caverns' action: put Gemstone Caverns onto the battlefield with a luck counter and exile a card from hand ([103.6a]). Adrian may choose the already-revealed Chancellor of the Annex as that exiled card; the card's own text only requires that it was revealed from the opening hand, and nothing conditions the effect on it staying in hand.

If Adrian exiles Chancellor of the Annex first, it is no longer in the opening hand and can no longer be revealed for its ability, so reveal first. Note [103.6b] says a revealed card stays revealed until the first turn begins; here Chancellor of the Annex simply leaves the hand for exile instead, and its granted effect remains in place.

Multiplayer: with more than two players, the revealed Chancellor of the Annex triggers separately for each opponent's first spell of the game, each of whom must pay {1} or have that spell countered ([Chancellor of the Annex ruling #1]). With exactly two players, only the single opponent is affected. Also, if Adrian somehow revealed two copies, each triggers and the opponent pays {1} that many times ([Chancellor of the Annex ruling #0]).

question: Aspen controls [Cosima, God of the Voyage] and mutates [Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt] onto it, putting it underneath Cosima, God of the Voyage. At the beginning of their next upkeep, Aspen exiles Cosima, God of the Voyage to its own triggered ability. What happens?
answer:
Aspen may exile the merged permanent, and doing so puts both physical cards — Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt — into exile as two separate cards. Only the Cosima, God of the Voyage card gains the delayed "voyage counter" ability, so when it later returns, it returns alone as a normal Cosima, God of the Voyage permanent; Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt stays in exile.

Details:

- The merged permanent is one permanent whose characteristics come from the top card, Cosima, God of the Voyage, and which has the abilities of both cards [702.140e]. So it has Cosima, God of the Voyage's upkeep trigger, Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's double strike, and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's "whenever this creature mutates" trigger (already used when the mutate resolved) [702.140d].
- When that trigger resolves and Aspen chooses to exile, the merged permanent leaves the battlefield: one permanent leaves, and each individual component card is put into the appropriate zone — here, exile. Because a player is exiling a merged permanent, Aspen determines the relative timestamp order of the cards at that time [730.3b]. An effect that can find the new object also finds all of those objects and takes the same action on each [730.3c].
- The exiled Cosima, God of the Voyage card is the object the ability grants the new triggered ability to ("it gains..."), so lands entering trigger it and voyage counters go on the Cosima, God of the Voyage card. When Aspen declines to add a counter, only Cosima, God of the Voyage returns to the battlefield, with X +1/+1 counters and X cards drawn [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #8]. Nothing in the provided rules re-merges the cards, so Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt remains exiled and Cosima, God of the Voyage no longer has double strike.
- If Aspen instead returned Cosima, God of the Voyage with no voyage counters, that's allowed; it just enters with no +1/+1 counters and no cards drawn [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #5].
- Timing note: I'm assuming the exile happens as the upkeep trigger resolves, which is the only time the choice is made [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #13] — the ability triggers only if the permanent is on the battlefield at the beginning of upkeep, and Aspen may exile only if it's still on the battlefield then.

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; none of the rules involved depend on the number of players.

question: Aubrey controls [Whiskervale Forerunner] and casts [Growth Cycle] to give it +3/+3. Before it resolves, Aubrey casts [Cooperate] choosing to copy Growth Cycle and changes the target to another creature. Does Whiskervale Forerunner trigger again?
answer:
No. Whiskervale Forerunner's valiant ability triggers only the first time each turn it becomes the target of a spell or ability you control, and that already happened when Aubrey cast Growth Cycle targeting it. Also, Aubrey changed the copy's target to a different creature, so the copy of Growth Cycle doesn't target Whiskervale Forerunner at all — two independent reasons there's no second trigger.

Details:
- Casting Growth Cycle targeting Whiskervale Forerunner triggers valiant; that trigger resolves before Growth Cycle itself does [Whiskervale Forerunner ruling #2].
- Cooperate creates a copy of Growth Cycle on the stack; the copy isn't cast, and you may choose new targets for it [707.10e], [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #11], [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #18]. A copy targeting a creature with valiant can trigger that creature's ability [Whiskervale Forerunner ruling #1] — but only if it hasn't already been targeted by a spell or ability you control this turn, which Whiskervale Forerunner has.
- So even if Aubrey had left the copy pointed at Whiskervale Forerunner, no new trigger would occur this turn.
- The copy resolves before the original Growth Cycle [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #14]. Each copy's bonus is locked in as it begins to resolve and counts only cards named Growth Cycle already in the graveyard at that time [Growth Cycle ruling #0], [Growth Cycle ruling #1] — the copy is not a card in the graveyard, so at that point the original Growth Cycle is still on the stack and adds nothing.

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Nico has a [Pillarfield Ox] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Arjun casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nico. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nico know which manifested card is which?
answer:
Direct answer: the three +1/+1 counters stay on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave the whole way (graveyard → exile → battlefield), so one of the manifested face-down permanents will be a 2/2 face-down creature with three +1/+1 counters on it — a 5/5. That visibly gives it away, so yes, everyone (including Nico) can tell which manifested card is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is Pillarfield Ox (the plain 2/2), even though the pile was shuffled.

Why the counters survive: normally counters simply cease to exist when an object changes zones ([122.2]). Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text overrides that general rule: "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Card text beats the general rule here. Ghastly Conscription moves it to exile and then to the battlefield — neither is a hand or library — so the counters ride along. Per [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1], the ability works because Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has that ability in the zone it's leaving (the graveyard, and then exile, where it is still just a face-down card, not an abilityless permanent). Per [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #0] those counters aren't "put" or "placed" on it, so counter-doubling/counter-hating effects don't interact with them. Per [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5] it retains all kinds of counters, not just +1/+1.

Other details:
- Ghastly Conscription's shuffle exists precisely to hide identities ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #3]), but power/toughness-modifying counters are public information on the battlefield, so the 5/5 is self-identifying.
- Arjun cast the spell, so Arjun manifests and controls both permanents; Arjun may look at them at any time ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #13]) and could turn the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card face up for {B}{G} as a special action any time Arjun has priority ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #2]).
- Face down, each permanent is a nameless, abilityless colorless 2/2 with mana value 0 ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #8]), so the face-down Skullbriar, the Walking Grave does not have its counter-retention ability while face down on the battlefield — meaning if it later leaves the battlefield while still face down, per [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1] it would lose those counters at that point.
- Note also [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #3]: it's a new object with no memory of its previous existence, but the counters still physically remain.

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided material is [Ghastly Conscription ruling #6]: if Arjun leaves the game, Nico's manifested cards are exiled.

It had the counters immediately before entering the battlefield however, so Nico will know which face-down permanent is the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is the Pillarfield Ox.

question: Avery activates [Ascendant Spirit]'s first ability. Before it resolves Avery casts [Slip Out the Back] targeting Ascendant Spirit. When it phases back in, what will it look like?
answer:
Ascendant Spirit phases back in during Avery's next untap step as a 1/1 Snow Creature — Spirit with one +1/+1 counter on it (so 2/2), *not* a Spirit Warrior with base 2/3.

Why: the stack resolves last-in-first-out, so Slip Out the Back (cast after the ability was activated) resolves first. It puts a +1/+1 counter on Ascendant Spirit and phases it out — "phased out" is a status meaning the game treats the permanent as though it doesn't exist [110.5c], [702.26c], [Slip Out the Back ruling #1]. When the {S}{S} ability of Ascendant Spirit then resolves, Ascendant Spirit is phased out and treated as nonexistent, so the ability does nothing to it; nothing sets its base power/toughness to 2/3 or makes it a Warrior [Slip Out the Back ruling #1]. Because the ability has no duration [Ascendant Spirit ruling #8], there's nothing left to "catch up" later.

Phasing back in: as a turn-based action at the start of Avery's next untap step, before Avery untaps permanents, all phased-out permanents that Avery controlled when they phased out phase in [502.1], [703.4a], [702.26a], [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. Counters are retained, so the +1/+1 counter is still there [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. Any Auras or Equipment that were attached phased out indirectly with it and phase in still attached [702.26g], [Slip Out the Back ruling #5]. It can attack and use {T} abilities that turn [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. Note also that nothing triggers from phasing out or in [Slip Out the Back ruling #3].

Assumed timing: the {S}{S} ability was still on the stack when Slip Out the Back resolved. If instead the {S}{S} ability had already resolved before Slip Out the Back resolved, Ascendant Spirit would phase in as a Spirit Warrior with base power/toughness 2/3 plus the +1/+1 counter (3/4), since that effect has no duration and characteristics/choices persist through phasing [Ascendant Spirit ruling #8], [Slip Out the Back ruling #4].

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games: the timing key is Avery's own untap step, not any opponent's.

question: Aspen controls [Parallel Lives] and a [Caldera Hellion]. They cast [Rite of Replication] targeting the Caldera Hellion. Can Aspen apply the devour replacement effect before the Parallel Lives replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
answer:
No. Aspen can't apply devour "first" in the sense they want: Parallel Lives' replacement effect must be applied before any of the tokens' devour effects, and even then a single creature can only be devoured by one token, not by each token.

Why Parallel Lives goes first: entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating a token, and when one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within it, the outer effect must be chosen first [616.1g]. So Rite of Replication's instruction to create a token that's a copy of Caldera Hellion is first modified by Parallel Lives, creating twice as many tokens (one becomes two; if Rite of Replication was kicked, five becomes ten) [Parallel Lives ruling #0]. Only after that do the individual tokens' "as this creature enters" devour effects get applied, in any order Aspen likes.

Why each token can't get a counter off one sacrifice: devour 1 means "as this creature enters, you may sacrifice any number of creatures; it enters with that many +1/+1 counters" [702.82c], and the choice is made before the token enters [614.12a]. The same object can't be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how permanents enter the battlefield [614.13b], and a creature you already control can be devoured by only one of the entering devour creatures [Caldera Hellion ruling #3]. The tokens also can't devour each other or themselves, since they're all entering simultaneously [614.13a, Caldera Hellion ruling #1]. So one sacrificed creature yields one +1/+1 counter on exactly one token.

Practically: Aspen's only creature to feed is the original Caldera Hellion (plus anything else they control). If they sacrifice it to one token, that token enters as a 3/3 with one +1/+1 counter (4/4) and the other token(s) enter as 3/3s with no counters. Then each token's "when this creature enters, it deals 3 damage to each creature" triggers resolve, and 3 damage from even one trigger is lethal to an uncountered 3/3 token [Caldera Hellion ruling #4] — with two or more tokens, the 4/4 dies too.

This answer doesn't depend on player count; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since Aspen is the affected object's controller making all these choices [616.1].

After that is applied the original Caldera Hellion's effect doesn't exist anymore, but each of the new Caldera Hellions entering the battlefield has its own effect, which can now be applied individually.

question: Aubrey controls [Exotic Orchard]. Nikolas controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Aubrey's Exotic Orchard produces no mana at all.

Why: Exotic Orchard reads "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce." The only ongoing mana ability of Nikolas's Crumbling Vestige is "{T}: Add {C}," and {C} is colorless mana specifically — colorless is not one of the five colors (white, blue, black, red, green). Exotic Orchard can never be tapped for colorless mana even when an opponent's land could produce colorless mana [Exotic Orchard ruling #3].

Crumbling Vestige's other ability, "When this land enters, add one mana of any color," is a triggered ability that only functions as Crumbling Vestige enters the battlefield; it isn't an ability that would produce mana if it resolved at the time Aubrey activates Exotic Orchard, so it doesn't define a color for the "could produce" check [106.7]. Costs and whether Crumbling Vestige is untapped are irrelevant to the check, but that doesn't help here [Exotic Orchard ruling #0].

Since no color of mana can be defined, the ability produces no mana instead of mana of an undefined type [106.5], [106.7]. Aubrey still taps Exotic Orchard (the cost is paid) and gets nothing.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as Aubrey activating Exotic Orchard at some point after Crumbling Vestige is already on the battlefield. If instead Aubrey somehow activated Exotic Orchard while Crumbling Vestige's enters-the-battlefield mana trigger were still pending, the answer would be the same for the activated-ability check described above, because that trigger resolves immediately on its own rather than being an ability Exotic Orchard evaluates as producible mana [605.4a].

Multiplayer note: Exotic Orchard looks at lands any opponent controls. In a two-player game Nikolas's Crumbling Vestige is the only land checked; at a larger table, if another opponent controlled, say, a Forest, Exotic Orchard could then produce {G} [Exotic Orchard ruling #4], [Forest].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.106.7: Some abilities produce mana based on the type of mana another permanent or permanents “could produce.” The type of mana a permanent could produce at any time includes any type of mana that an ability of that permanent would produce if the ability were to resolve at that time, taking into account any applicable replacement effects in any possible order. Ignore whether any costs of the ability could or could not be paid. If that permanent wouldn’t produce any mana under these conditions, or no type of mana can be defined this way, there’s no type of mana it could produce. Exotic Orchard has the ability “{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce.” If your opponent controls no lands, activating Exotic Orchard’s mana ability will produce no mana. The same is true if you and your opponent each control no lands other than Exotic Orchards. However, if you control a Forest and an Exotic Orchard, and your opponent controls an Exotic Orchard, then each Exotic Orchard could produce {G}.

Add one mana of that color.” If you control no colored permanents, activating Meteor Crater’s mana ability produces no mana.

However, if you control a Forest and an Exotic Orchard, and your opponent controls an Exotic Orchard, then each Exotic Orchard could produce {G}.

Rather, it resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority. An enchantment reads, “Whenever a player taps a land for mana, that player adds one mana of any type that land produced.” If a player taps lands for mana while casting a spell, the additional mana is added immediately and can be used to pay for the spell.

answer_gold: Any color. Exotic Orchard checks to see what mana Crumbling Vestige could produce if any of its abilities were to resolve at that time. That includes triggered abilities.

question: Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan are playing a multiplayer game. Beckham controls [Stalking Leonin]. Azariah casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Beckham's next turn. After Beckham begins their turn, can Azariah see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
answer:
Yes. Azariah gets to see which opponent Beckham secretly chose for Stalking Leonin.

While controlling another player, you see all information in the game that the controlled player can see [723.4], [Worst Fears ruling #11] — that expressly includes cards in Beckham's hand, face-down permanents Beckham controls, and any hidden game information Beckham has access to. The secret choice recorded for Stalking Leonin (e.g., a name written on a slip of paper kept with the card, per [Stalking Leonin ruling #2]) is information about an object in the game that is visible to Beckham, so during the controlled turn it is visible to Azariah as well.

Two limits worth noting:
- Azariah still doesn't control Stalking Leonin itself; only control of the player changes [723.3], [Worst Fears ruling #4]. But Azariah makes Beckham's decisions, so Azariah decides whether to activate Stalking Leonin's "Reveal the player you chose" ability during that turn, using only Beckham's resources [723.5b], [Worst Fears ruling #8]. The choice that matters is the one Beckham made when Stalking Leonin entered; Azariah cannot change it, since Azariah can't make choices not called for by the rules or cards [723.5b], [Worst Fears ruling #2].
- The exception in [723.4] is information about cards outside the game (like a sideboard) — that stays hidden from Azariah [Worst Fears ruling #12]. A secret in-game choice is not that.

This is the same in a two-player game as at this three-player table; with three players, Caelan is unaffected and learns nothing, and note that Stalking Leonin's ability only exiles an attacking creature controlled by the chosen player and only if it's attacking Beckham (not a planeswalker) [Stalking Leonin ruling #4]. If Beckham had multiple Stalking Leonins, each could have a different chosen opponent, and Azariah would see each of those recorded choices [Stalking Leonin ruling #1].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.722.4: In every zone, a preparation card has only its normal characteristics.

cited_text.723.4: If information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it’s visible to both that player and the controller of the player. If information about cards outside the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it’s visible only to that player, not the controller of the player. The controller of a player can see that player’s hand and the face of any face-down creatures they control.
cited_text.723.3: Only control of the player changes. All objects are controlled by their normal controllers. A player who’s being controlled during their turn is still the active player.
cited_text.723.5b: While controlling another player, a player makes all choices and decisions the controlled player is allowed to make or is told to make by the rules or by any objects. This includes choices and decisions about what to play, and choices and decisions called for by spells and abilities. The controller of another player can’t make choices or decisions for that player that aren’t called for by the rules or by any objects. The controller also can’t make any choices or decisions for the player that would be called for by the tournament rules. The player who’s being controlled still decides if they will leave to visit the restroom, trade a card to someone else, agree to an intentional draw, or call a judge about an error or infraction.

answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Beckham. Azariah can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

question: Angela controls [Mirror Gallery] and two [Sakashima the Impostor]s. One is a copy of their [Master of the Hunt]; the other is copying a wolf token created by Master of the Hunt. They attack with all four creatures. What are the possible bands that Angela may declare?
answer:
Angela can't declare any meaningful band — no legal band of two or more creatures exists here, so all four creatures attack as individuals.

Why:

1. None of the four attackers has plain banding. Master of the Hunt (and Sakashima the Impostor copying Master of the Hunt) only has an activated ability that creates Wolves of the Hunt tokens with "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt"; the ability doesn't give Master of the Hunt itself banding, and copies don't share abilities of other creatures (702.22g). So the first kind of band in 702.22c (one or more creatures with banding plus up to one without) is unavailable.

2. That leaves the "bands with other [quality]" band, where the quality is "named Wolves of the Hunt." Rule 702.22c requires one or more attacking [quality] creatures with "bands with other [quality]" plus any number of other attacking [quality] creatures — every member of such a band must itself have the quality.

3. The Sakashima the Impostor that copied the Wolves of the Hunt token does have the ability "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt," but its own copy effect specifies that its name is still Sakashima the Impostor. So that Sakashima the Impostor is not a creature named Wolves of the Hunt and cannot be a member of a "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt" band — neither as the ability-holder nor as another band member.

4. The only attacker actually named Wolves of the Hunt is the single original token. A "band" of just that one creature accomplishes nothing (banding matters only for blocking/damage among multiple band members, per 702.22h and 702.22i).

Mirror Gallery is only relevant for letting Angela keep two Sakashima the Impostor permanents (and a legendary Master of the Hunt copy) on the battlefield at once, since the "legend rule" doesn't apply while Mirror Gallery is on the battlefield; it has no effect on band legality.

If Angela first activated Master of the Hunt (or the Sakashima the Impostor copying it) to make a second Wolves of the Hunt token and attacked with those, then the two or more creatures named Wolves of the Hunt could form a band, since at least one of them has "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt."

Timing/attack-target note: bands are declared as part of declaring attackers (508.1e), and all creatures in a band must attack the same player, planeswalker, or battle (702.22d, 802.3b). In a two-player game that's automatic; with more than two players (or multiple planeswalkers/battles), Angela couldn't split a band across different defending players even if a legal band existed.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

A player may declare as many attacking bands as they want, but each creature may be a member of only one of them. (Defending players can’t declare bands but may use banding in a different way; see rule 702.22j.)

answer_gold: No bands can be declared. The only creature on the battlefield named "Wolves of the Hunt" is the token, so it cannot declare itself as in a band with anything else. The Sakashima the Impostor with "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt" is not itself named "Wolves of the Hunt", so it cannot declare itself as in a band with the token.

question: Avery controls a Germ token that's equipped with [Barbed Bloodletter]. Nadia controls two [Teferi's Curse]s, one on the Germ, the other on the Barbed Bloodletter. During Avery's untap step, which permanents will phase out? Which of these will phase back in?
answer:
All four permanents phase out during Avery's untap step, and none of them phase back in during that same untap step — they all phase back in during Avery's next untap step.

Details:

1. Phasing is a static ability that modifies the untap step: during each player's untap step, before that player untaps, all phased-in permanents with phasing that player controls phase out, and all phased-out permanents that had phased out under that player's control phase in — simultaneously [702.26a] [502.1] [703.4a].
2. The Germ token has phasing (granted by the Teferi's Curse enchanting it) and Avery controls it, so the Germ token phases out. Barbed Bloodletter also has phasing (granted by the other Teferi's Curse) and Avery controls it, so Barbed Bloodletter phases out directly as well. Note that the controller of Teferi's Curse (Nadia) is irrelevant — what matters is who controls the permanent that has the phasing ability.
3. Both copies of Teferi's Curse phase out at the same time, "indirectly," because Auras attached to a permanent that phases out phase out with it [702.26g]. Teferi's Curse itself does not have phasing.
4. Nothing phases in this untap step, since none of these permanents were already phased out before Avery's untap step began.
5. On Avery's next untap step: the Germ token phases in (it phased out under Avery's control), and Barbed Bloodletter phases in as well, since it phased out directly under Avery's control [702.26a]. Each Teferi's Curse phases in along with the permanent it's attached to, rather than by itself [702.26g], and Barbed Bloodletter phases in still attached to the Germ token.
6. While phased out, the Germ token keeps existing (tokens aren't destroyed by phasing) and no zone-change or attach/unattach triggers occur [702.26d] [702.26j]. The wither granted by Barbed Bloodletter's enters trigger is an "until end of turn" effect and will already have ended in the cleanup step of the earlier turn [514.2].
7. Caveat: if an effect makes Avery skip their untap step, the phasing event simply doesn't happen that turn [702.26m].

Multiplayer: the answer is the same at any table size, since phasing keys off the controller of the phasing permanent. One multiplayer-only wrinkle: if Nadia left the game while a Teferi's Curse (or anything else) was phased out under her control, a permanent that phased out under a departed player's control phases in during the next untap step after that player's next turn would have begun [702.26n].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.26d: Phasing The phasing event doesn’t actually cause a permanent to change zones or control, even though it’s treated as though it’s not on the battlefield and not under its controller’s control while it’s phased out. Zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out. Tokens continue to exist on the battlefield while phased out. Counters and stickers remain on a permanent while it’s phased out. Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

This all happens simultaneously. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. See rule 702.26, “Phasing.”

This all happens simultaneously. See rule 502.1.
