question: Nehemiah controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ari casts [Bishop of Binding], exiling the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. When Ari attacks with Bishop of Binding on their next turn, what will X equal in Bishop of Binding's triggered ability?
answer:
X will be 3.

Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is printed 1/1 and had 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Normally, [Bishop of Binding ruling #1] says any counters on the creature exiled by Bishop of Binding cease to exist — but Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text reads "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is not a hand or library, so the counters stay, and that specific card text overrides the general behavior described in the ruling.

Because +1/+1 counters modify power and toughness even in zones other than the battlefield ([122.1a], and confirmed by [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2], which notes a Skullbriar in the command zone with a +1/+1 counter is 2/2), the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card in exile is 3/3. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave also had the relevant ability in the zone it left (the battlefield), which is what [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1] requires.

Bishop of Binding's attack trigger sets X to the power of the exiled card, and that value is determined only as the ability resolves ([Bishop of Binding ruling #5]). So as it resolves on Ari's next turn, X = 3, and the target Vampire gets +3/+3 until end of turn. Caveats: if Bishop of Binding leaves the battlefield before the attack trigger resolves, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave returns and there is no exiled card, making X = 0 ([Bishop of Binding ruling #0]). If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave gained or lost counters in the meantime, use its power at resolution.

Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Bishop of Binding just targets a creature an opponent controls.

question: Neriah controls a [Containment Priest] and has a [Knotvine Mystic] in their graveyard. Alan casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Neriah. What happens to the Knotvine Mystic?
answer:
Knotvine Mystic never actually arrives on the battlefield — Containment Priest exiles it instead.

Step by step: Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from Neriah's graveyard face down, shuffles that pile, then manifests those cards. Manifesting means putting a card onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature (with no name, mana cost, or abilities, colorless, mana value 0) — it is not cast (see Ghastly Conscription ruling #8, and [701.62a] for the manifest-dread reference to manifesting). Containment Priest reads "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead." Knotvine Mystic is a nontoken card entering as a face-down 2/2 creature without having been cast, so Containment Priest's replacement effect applies and Knotvine Mystic goes to exile instead of the battlefield. Containment Priest ruling #1 confirms the ability only spares creatures that were actually cast, and ruling #3 confirms what matters is whether the object is a creature as it enters — a face-down manifested permanent is a creature, so it's caught.

Note that this happens even though Alan cast Ghastly Conscription and would have controlled the manifested permanents; Containment Priest's ability isn't limited to its controller's creatures. Any other creature cards from Neriah's graveyard manifested by the same spell are exiled the same way. Because Knotvine Mystic was already exiled face down by Ghastly Conscription and Containment Priest simply exiles it instead of letting it enter, it stays in exile — it does not return to Neriah's graveyard.

Player count doesn't change this: Ghastly Conscription targets a single player, and Containment Priest's ability applies to every nontoken creature that would enter without being cast, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Avery controls [Magnetic Web] and is attacking with two [Leatherback Baloth]s with magnet counters on them. Nayeli controls one [Imperial Moth] that also has a magnet counter on it. What are Nayeli's legal blocks?
answer:
Nayeli must block with Imperial Moth, and she may choose either one of the two Leatherback Baloths — blocking neither is illegal, and she can only satisfy one of the two requirements.

Why: Magnetic Web's triggered ability ("Whenever a creature with a magnet counter on it attacks, all creatures with magnet counters on them block that creature this turn if able") triggers once for each attacking Leatherback Baloth, so there are two separate blocking requirements on Imperial Moth, which has a magnet counter. Requirements are checked under rule 509.1c: the declaration is illegal if the number of requirements obeyed is fewer than the maximum possible number that could be obeyed without violating any restriction. Since Imperial Moth is a single creature that can block only one attacker (509.1a — each blocking creature is assigned to one attacking creature), the maximum obtainable is one requirement. So blocking one Leatherback Baloth is legal (either one), and declaring no blocks is illegal.

Imperial Moth having flying is no obstacle: flying restricts what can block a flier, not what a flier may block (509.1b concerns evasion restrictions on attackers). Neither Leatherback Baloth has an evasion ability here.

Also note Magnetic Web's first ability forced both Leatherback Baloths to attack if able — that's why both are attacking; it doesn't change the block analysis.

Multiplayer note: Nayeli can only block creatures attacking her, a planeswalker she controls, or a battle she protects (509.1a, 802.4a). If more than one player is being attacked, each defending player declares blockers in APNAP order, and when checking legality you ignore attackers aimed at other players and other players' blockers (802.4b). So if one Leatherback Baloth were attacking a different player, only one requirement would apply to Nayeli, and Imperial Moth would have to block that Leatherback Baloth attacking Nayeli.

question: Arden controls [Naga Vitalist] and a [Deathrite Shaman] that's currently a land due to [Xenograft] (naming "Saproling") and [Life and Limb]. Neither player has any land cards in their graveyards. If Arden taps Naga Vitalist, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Arden can only produce {G}.

Why: Xenograft naming "Saproling" makes each creature Arden controls a Saproling in addition to its other types, so Deathrite Shaman (and Naga Vitalist itself) are Saprolings [Xenograft, Xenograft ruling #1]. Life and Limb then makes all Saprolings 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types, so Deathrite Shaman is a land with the Forest subtype [Life and Limb, Life and Limb ruling #3]. Any land with the Forest subtype has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6, Life and Limb ruling #2, Forest].

Naga Vitalist's ability adds one mana of any type a land you control "could produce." The types of mana are white, blue, black, red, green, and colorless [Naga Vitalist ruling #2]. Arden controls lands whose only mana ability is "{T}: Add {G}" (Deathrite Shaman as a Forest land, and Naga Vitalist itself if it is also a Forest land), so the only type available is green.

Deathrite Shaman's first ability ("{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color.") does not add any colors to that list here. Rule 106.7 tells you to ignore whether the ability's costs could be paid [106.7, Naga Vitalist ruling #0], but the ability still requires a target land card in a graveyard; with no land cards in any graveyard the ability could not resolve and would produce no mana, so no color of mana can be defined from it [Deathrite Shaman ruling #0]. Also note that ability is not even a mana ability because it targets [Deathrite Shaman ruling #1]. Mana of an undefined type is simply no mana [106.5].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming both Xenograft (with Saproling chosen) and Life and Limb are already on the battlefield and resolved when Naga Vitalist is tapped. If Life and Limb weren't in play, Deathrite Shaman would not be a land at all and Naga Vitalist would look only at Arden's other lands.

Player count doesn't matter: Naga Vitalist checks only lands you control, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game (the "no land cards in graveyards" condition just needs to hold for every graveyard for Deathrite Shaman's targeted ability).

question: Adelyn controls [Panharmonicon] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and has [Dwarven Trader] and [Staunch Shieldmate] in their graveyard. They cast [Animate Dead] targeting Dwarven Trader. What happens as it enters the battlefield?
answer:
Adelyn's Animate Dead enters the battlefield attached to Dwarven Trader in the graveyard, and its enters-the-battlefield triggered ability triggers twice instead of once (thanks to Panharmonicon), but only the first instance actually does anything: Dwarven Trader comes back to the battlefield under Adelyn's control with Animate Dead attached to it. Staunch Shieldmate stays in the graveyard.

Why Panharmonicon applies: Mycosynth Lattice says "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types," so once Animate Dead is on the battlefield it is an artifact permanent (Mycosynth Lattice does not make the Animate Dead spell on the stack an artifact — [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1]). Panharmonicon reads "If an artifact or creature entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time," and it applies to a permanent's own enters-the-battlefield trigger and to a permanent entering at the same time as the trigger source ([Panharmonicon ruling #4], [Panharmonicon ruling #1]). So Animate Dead's own "When this Aura enters..." ability triggers twice.

What each instance does:
- First instance: the intervening-if clause is satisfied (Animate Dead is on the battlefield), it swaps its enchant ability for "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," returns Dwarven Trader to the battlefield under Adelyn's control, and reattaches itself to that new object ([Animate Dead ruling #1]). Dwarven Trader gets -1/-0, so it's a 0/1.
- Second instance: Animate Dead is no longer attached to a creature card in a graveyard — the card it was tracking is now a permanent on the battlefield, so the ability can't find it in the graveyard it left and that part of the ability does nothing ([603.6a]). Panharmonicon does not copy the ability or let Adelyn make a new choice of card, so it cannot instead reanimate Staunch Shieldmate; choices are made per instance but the ability isn't retargeted at a new graveyard card ([Panharmonicon ruling #8]).

Other notes: Panharmonicon never affects replacement or "as it enters" effects ([Panharmonicon ruling #0], [Panharmonicon ruling #7]), so nothing about how Animate Dead or Dwarven Trader enters is doubled. Dwarven Trader entering is itself an artifact-and-creature entering (via Mycosynth Lattice), so any other enters-triggers Adelyn controls would also be doubled — here there are none. Mycosynth Lattice also makes everything colorless ([Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2]), which is irrelevant to legality here since Dwarven Trader has no protection issue ([Animate Dead ruling #0]).

Assumed timing: both trigger instances go on the stack together and resolve one at a time, with Adelyn choosing their order; since they're identical, the order doesn't change the outcome. This works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game — nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Continuous effects that modify characteristics of permanents do so simultaneously with the permanent entering the battlefield. They don’t wait until the permanent is on the battlefield and then change it. Because such effects apply as the permanent enters the battlefield, they are applied before determining whether the permanent will cause an ability to trigger when it enters the battlefield. A permanent with the static ability “All white creatures get +1/+1” is on the battlefield. A creature spell that would normally create a 1/1 white creature instead creates a 2/2 white creature. The creature doesn’t enter the battlefield as 1/1 and then change to 2/2.

During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Enters-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent enters the battlefield. These are written, “When [this object] enters, . . . “ or “Whenever a [type] enters, . . .” Each time an event puts one or more permanents onto the battlefield, all permanents on the battlefield (including the newcomers) are checked for any enters-the-battlefield triggers that match the event.

answer_gold: Animate Dead enters the battlefield attached to Dwarven Trader and triggers twice. The first trigger will return Dwarven Trader to the battlefield. The second trigger just does the same things again, so it has no relevant result.

question: Armani controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 3 [Canopy Vista]s. Nico controls a [Reverence] and 1 Canopy Vista. Can Armani attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
Yes — Armani can declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Nico.

Why: Reverence's restriction is "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you," and restrictions are checked when attackers are declared [508.1c]. At that moment Gaea's Liege is not yet attacking, so it uses its "isn't attacking" characteristic-defining values: power and toughness each equal the number of Forests Armani controls. Armani's 3 Canopy Vistas each have the Forest land type (they're nonbasic, but they are Forests) [Canopy Vista ruling #0], so Gaea's Liege is 3/3 at declaration. 3 is greater than 2, so Reverence doesn't stop the attack. Gaea's Liege's ruling states this explicitly: use the "not attacking" power and toughness when it's being declared as an attacker; it only changes after declaration is complete [Gaea's Liege ruling #0].

Once the declaration is complete, Gaea's Liege becomes attacking and its power/toughness become the number of Forests the defending player (Nico) controls — 1 Canopy Vista, so 1/1. That does not retroactively make the attack illegal, because Reverence's restriction is only applied during the declaration of attackers [508.1c]. It does mean Gaea's Liege will deal only 1 damage and dies to 1 damage.

Multiplayer note: with only two players, Nico is the sole defending player. At a larger table, all of Armani's opponents are defending players [802.2a], Armani could instead send Gaea's Liege at another opponent (in which case its attacking power equals that player's Forests) subject to seating/range restrictions [801.3], and Reverence would only protect Nico — a creature that can't attack Nico may still attack a planeswalker Nico controls [Reverence ruling #0].

question: Ariel attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Charnel Serenade]?
answer:
No. As Wildfire Eternal's triggered ability resolves, Ariel cannot suspend Charnel Serenade; they may only cast an instant or sorcery from hand without paying its mana cost, or decline.

Why:
- Suspending is not casting. Exiling a card with suspend is a special action ([116.2f], [Charnel Serenade ruling #15]) — it doesn't use the stack ([405.6d]) and can be taken only when the player has priority. No player has priority in the middle of resolving Wildfire Eternal's trigger, so the special action isn't available at that moment.
- Wildfire Eternal's ability grants permission to "cast an instant or sorcery spell from your hand without paying its mana cost," which is a different thing from taking suspend's special action.
- Even if Ariel instead uses that permission to cast Charnel Serenade itself, they can't use suspend as part of that: suspend's casting is done via alternative costs ([702.62d]), and a card cast "without paying its mana cost" can't have alternative costs paid ([Wildfire Eternal ruling #6], [Charnel Serenade ruling #4]).

What Ariel can do: cast Charnel Serenade from hand for free as the trigger resolves — sorcery timing is fine here ([Wildfire Eternal ruling #0], and the trigger happens in the declare blockers step per [Wildfire Eternal ruling #4]). Charnel Serenade's own text then surveils 3, returns a creature card from the graveyard with a finality counter, and exiles Charnel Serenade with three time counters — so it ends up suspended anyway as part of its resolution, just not by the suspend special action.

Ariel can, of course, suspend Charnel Serenade by paying {2}{B} at a later moment when they hold priority and could begin to cast it (i.e., a main phase of their own turn, since it's a sorcery) ([702.62a], [702.62c], [Charnel Serenade ruling #10]).

This analysis is unaffected by player count — it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Timing note: I'm assuming the question means "during the resolution of the trigger." If instead Ariel means after the trigger has finished resolving and they regain priority, they still couldn't suspend Charnel Serenade then, because it's a sorcery and it isn't a main phase with an empty stack — you'd need to be able to begin casting it ([702.62a]).

question: Brynn has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Fairgrounds Warden] that exiled Coleman's [Alpha Tyrranax]. Aspen casts [Psychic Purge], targeting Brynn. What happens as Brynn loses the game?
answer:
Alpha Tyrranax stays in exile permanently. Psychic Purge deals 1 damage to Brynn, dropping Brynn to 0 life, so Brynn loses and leaves the game. Every object Brynn owns leaves the game, and that expressly includes phased-out permanents such as Fairgrounds Warden — but a phased-out permanent leaving the game this way is *not* a "leaves the battlefield" event, so the condition on Fairgrounds Warden's exile effect ("until this creature leaves the battlefield") is never met and Coleman's Alpha Tyrranax never returns.

Details and definitions:
- "Phased out" means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist, but it is still on the battlefield. Rule [702.26k] says phased-out permanents owned by a player who leaves the game also leave the game, and that this doesn't cause zone-change abilities to trigger.
- The definition of "leaves the battlefield" [Leaves the Battlefield] covers a permanent moving from the battlefield to another zone, or leaving the game because its owner leaves the game *only if it's phased in*. Fairgrounds Warden is phased out here, so no leave-the-battlefield event occurs, and the exile duration never ends. This is the key difference from [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #0], which assumes a phased-in Fairgrounds Warden whose owner leaves the game (there, the return happens, and it happens even though it's a one-shot effect rather than a stack ability).
- Note that if Alpha Tyrranax had been a token rather than a card, it would already have ceased to exist and could not return anyway [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #1].
- All of this happens immediately, without using the stack, as Brynn leaves the game [800.4a], [405.6h].
- Abilities that trigger when a player loses the game do trigger here ("looking back in time" to see Brynn and Brynn's permanents as they were just before the event) [603.9], [603.10f]. Any triggered ability that would be controlled by Brynn is not put on the stack at all [800.4d].

Assumed timing: I'm reading this as Psychic Purge resolving and dealing the damage, with the 0-life loss detected as a state-based action immediately after. Psychic Purge's own "that player loses 5 life" clause is irrelevant since nobody is being made to discard it.

Multiplayer vs. two players: this answer is for the multiplayer table implied by three named players — the game continues after Brynn leaves [800.4a]. With only two players, Brynn's loss simply ends the game and none of this cleanup matters.

question: Avery controls [Caelorna, Coral Tyrant] and [Darksteel Garrison] that's fortifying [Spire Garden]. Avery casts [Bludgeon Brawl]. After that resolves they activate Darksteel Garrison's equip ability targeting Caelorna, Coral Tyrant. What does the battlefield look like after that ability has resolved and state-based actions have been checked?
answer:
After the equip resolves, Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant and is no longer attached to Spire Garden, and state-based actions leave it there.

Why:

1. Bludgeon Brawl says "Each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact is an Equipment with equip {X} and 'Equipped creature gets +X/+0,' where X is that artifact's mana value." Darksteel Garrison is an artifact — Fortification, is not a creature, and is not already an Equipment, so it qualifies. Its mana value is 2, so it gains equip {2} (two generic mana, payable with any colors or colorless) and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0." It keeps its other types and abilities, so it is still a Fortification with its fortify {3} ability and its two fortified-land abilities [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #0 does not apply here; see Bludgeon Brawl ruling #0/#1 on the trigger, and Bludgeon Brawl ruling #0 about retained types — specifically Bludgeon Brawl ruling #0 in the artifact list].
2. Equip moves the Equipment to the target creature. Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is a creature, which is a legal object for an Equipment to be attached to (301.5c), and an object can only be attached to one thing, so Darksteel Garrison stops fortifying Spire Garden.
3. Nothing unattaches it afterward: Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is a legal permanent for an Equipment (301.5c), and Darksteel Garrison is not a creature itself, so the "an Equipment that's also a creature can't equip" restriction doesn't bite (301.5c, Bludgeon Brawl ruling #3). State-based actions only unattach an Equipment/Fortification when it's attached to something illegal (704.5p, 801.9).
4. Result: Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is a 2/8 (0/8 with +2/+0) and is "modified" because it is equipped [Modified]. Its Fortification abilities do nothing while there is no fortified land, so Spire Garden is no longer indestructible and no longer triggers the +1/+1 ability when it becomes tapped (Darksteel Garrison ruling #1, ruling #3 no longer protect it).

Assumption on timing: I'm reading it as Bludgeon Brawl fully resolving before the equip activation, as stated. If Bludgeon Brawl were somehow no longer on the battlefield when the equip resolved, Darksteel Garrison would lose the Equipment subtype and become unattached, remaining on the battlefield (Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2).

Player count: none of this depends on the number of opponents. The only opponent-count-sensitive text here is Spire Garden's "enters tapped unless you have two or more opponents," which only matters as it entered the battlefield (Spire Garden ruling #0), not now.

Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant and not to Spire Garden.

When its equip ability resolves, it becomes attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant.

question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?
answer:
Yes. Nico can legally target Pristine Angel with Murder, and Murder will resolve and destroy it.

Why: Cephalid Snitch's ability said "Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn," and it resolved while Pristine Angel was tapped (and therefore a legal target, since a tapped Pristine Angel has no protection at all). That is a continuous effect lasting until end of turn; it is not tied to Pristine Angel's tapped status. When Abel casts a spell and uses Pristine Angel's triggered ability to untap it, Pristine Angel regains protection from artifacts and from each color — except black, which the still-active Cephalid Snitch effect keeps stripping for the rest of the turn. So Murder, a black instant, isn't stopped by protection: Pristine Angel is a legal target on announcement, and it's still a legal target when Murder checks targets on resolution [608.2b].

Two side notes:
- Untapping Pristine Angel does not remove it from combat, so it's still an attacking creature until Murder kills it [506.4b].
- Nico targeting a permanent Abel controls commits a crime, which matters only if some card cares about that [700.13], [Crime].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability fully resolved while Pristine Angel was tapped, exactly as stated. If instead Pristine Angel had been untapped when Nico tried to activate Cephalid Snitch's ability targeting it, Pristine Angel's protection from each color would have made it an illegal target for that ability (Cephalid Snitch is blue), and Murder would likewise be unable to target it. Also, if Cephalid Snitch's ability were still on the stack when Pristine Angel untapped, the ability would be countered on resolution for having no legal target [608.2b].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players; the protection and targeting analysis is identical, and the crime rule simply asks whether the target is controlled by an opponent [700.13].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.613.7a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. A continuous effect generated by a static ability has the same timestamp as the object the static ability is on, or the timestamp of the effect that created the ability, whichever is later. If the effect that created the ability has the later timestamp and the object the ability is on receives a new timestamp, each continuous effect generated by static abilities of that object receives a new timestamp as well, but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same. Rune of Flight is an Aura that grants enchanted Equipment “Equipped creature has flying.” A player attaches Rune of Flight to Colossus Hammer, an Equipment with “Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying.” The ability granted by Rune of Flight shares Rune of Flight’s timestamp because it is later than Colossus Hammer’s timestamp. If Colossus Hammer becomes attached to a creature, both of its abilities receive new timestamps (see rule 613.7e), but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same.

Plague Spores still resolves because the black creature land is still a legal target for the “target land” part of the spell. The “destroy target nonblack creature” part of the spell won’t affect that permanent, but the “destroy target land” part of the spell will still destroy it. It can’t be regenerated.

answer_gold:
Yes. "Protection from all colors" is shorthand for protection from each color individually. It loses protection from black, and still has protection from all the other colors.

question: Adelyn controls [Back from the Brink] and has [Shifting Wall] in their graveyard. Can Adelyn activate Back from the Brink's ability to create a token of Shifting Wall? Can they pay more than {0} to do so? If so, will it enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Yes, Adelyn can activate Back from the Brink exiling Shifting Wall, but X is treated as zero, so the mana cost paid is {0} — Adelyn cannot choose a larger value. The token enters with zero +1/+1 counters and, as a 0/0, is put into the graveyard immediately as a state-based action.

Why: Back from the Brink says "Exile a creature card from your graveyard and pay its mana cost: Create a token that's a copy of that card. Activate only as a sorcery." Shifting Wall's mana cost is {X}, and per [Back from the Brink ruling #3], if the exiled creature card has {X} in its mana cost, X is considered to be zero. There's no choice to pay more; you aren't casting the card, so nothing lets Adelyn set X higher ([Back from the Brink ruling #1]).

Shifting Wall's "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it" is a replacement effect that does apply to the token — copy effects and Back from the Brink both preserve "enters with" abilities ([Back from the Brink ruling #2], [707.5]) — but with X = 0 it puts on no counters. The token is therefore a 0/0 Artifact Creature — Wall with defender and dies right away.

Timing: the ability can only be activated during Adelyn's main phase when the stack is empty ("Activate only as a sorcery"). Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

In that case, the value of X is the value chosen or determined for it as the spell was cast.

question: Alex controls a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], a [Mycosynth Lattice], and a [Control Magic] that took control of a [Boris Devilboon] from Nico. Alex begins activating the ability of Boris Devilboon and sacrifices Control Magic to help pay the cost. Is this legal? If so, who will control the ability?
answer:
Yes, it's legal, and Alex controls the ability.

Why it's legal: Alex controls Boris Devilboon (Control Magic says "You control enchanted creature," a control-changing effect applied in layer 2), so Alex is the player allowed to activate Boris Devilboon's activated ability [602.2, 701.2a, 613.1b]. Activating puts the ability on the stack and then costs are paid; Alex may activate mana abilities during that payment. Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts, so Control Magic (an Aura enchantment) is also an artifact and is a legal thing to sacrifice to Krark-Clan Ironworks [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3 confirms Auras become artifacts]. Sacrificing Control Magic to Krark-Clan Ironworks adds {C}{C}, and Mycosynth Lattice lets players spend mana as though it were mana of any color, so that colorless mana can pay the {B} and {R} in Boris Devilboon's cost of {2}{B}{R} [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #0, Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2]. Boris Devilboon's cost also includes {T}, which Alex pays by tapping Boris Devilboon while still controlling it. Note you'd need two Krark-Clan Ironworks activations (4 mana) to cover {2}{B}{R} in total: two for the generic {2}, one each for {B} and {R}.

Who controls the ability: the controller of an activated ability on the stack is the player who activated it — Alex — and that never changes afterward [113.8]. Once Control Magic is sacrificed, control of Boris Devilboon reverts to Nico, but the ability already on the stack stays Alex's, so Alex creates the Minor Demon token under Alex's control. Because Boris Devilboon left Alex's control after the ability was already activated and paid for, nothing is rewound; announcements and payments can't be altered once made [602.2].

One timing note: this assumes Control Magic is sacrificed during the payment step of activating Boris Devilboon's ability (i.e., after the ability is on the stack). If instead Alex sacrificed Control Magic first and then tried to activate Boris Devilboon's ability, Alex would no longer control Boris Devilboon and could not activate it at all [602.2, 701.2a].

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; the only difference is which opponent's card Control Magic was taking.

question: Nico has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Aiden controls a [Chronatog Totem] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts an [Evil Twin], choosing to have it copy Chronatog Totem. What happens?
answer:
Evil Twin enters the battlefield under Nico's control, and Nico — not Aiden — chooses what it copies. It will be a copy of the printed Chronatog Totem: a noncreature artifact (not a 1/2 Atog creature), because the animation effect isn't copied.

Step by step:

1. Gather Specimens says a creature that would enter under an opponent's control enters under your control instead. Evil Twin is a creature spell, so as it would enter under Aiden's control, Nico's Gather Specimens redirects it; Gather Specimens isn't targeted and applies to creatures entering by any means [Gather Specimens ruling #4, Gather Specimens ruling #7].
2. Gather Specimens' replacement effect is applied before other effects that modify how the permanent enters, including copy choices — the ruling explicitly says that if Clone would enter under an opponent's control, *you* choose which creature it copies as it enters under your control [Gather Specimens ruling #3]. So Aiden's declared choice of Chronatog Totem doesn't bind Nico; Nico makes the "as it enters" copy choice (and could even choose nothing, leaving a 0/0 that dies) [Evil Twin ruling #4]. The order of applying replacement effects generally belongs to the affected object's controller [616.1f].
3. Assuming Nico chooses Chronatog Totem: copiable values are only what's printed on the card, as modified by other copy effects; type-changing effects like Chronatog Totem's own "{1}{U}: This artifact becomes a 1/2 blue Atog artifact creature until end of turn" are NOT copied [707.2]. So Nico's Evil Twin is an artifact named Chronatog Totem with no power/toughness and is not a creature — it doesn't die as a 0/0. It has "{T}: Add {U}", the {1}{U} animation ability, and the {0} +3/+3-skip-a-turn ability.
4. As a copy modification, it also gains "{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature" [707.9b, Evil Twin ruling #0]. Its name is Chronatog Totem, so Nico can use that ability to destroy Aiden's Chronatog Totem — but only once Nico can legally tap it. Since Nico's copy is not a creature, tap abilities are fine only if Nico has controlled the permanent since the beginning of Nico's most recent turn; it just entered, so Nico must wait [Chronatog Totem ruling #0]. If Nico animates it with {1}{U}, it's then a creature that also can't tap or attack this turn.
5. Any enters-the-battlefield triggers of the copied card would trigger for Nico; Chronatog Totem has none [Evil Twin ruling #6, Gather Specimens ruling #6].

Multiplayer note: this works the same at any table size, since Gather Specimens affects creatures entering under *any* opponent's control [Gather Specimens ruling #4]. If another player had also cast Gather Specimens this turn, the would-be controller chooses which one to apply, then the new would-be controller chooses among the rest, and so on [Gather Specimens ruling #5, Gather Specimens ruling #8].

question: Albert and Nico are beginning the game and have just drawn 7 cards. Albert has [Serum Powder] in their hand. Does Albert get to know whether Nico is going to mulligan before deciding whether to use Serum Powder's ability?
answer:
It depends on who's the starting player, because Serum Powder's ability is used at the moment you would declare whether you're taking a mulligan.

- If Nico is the starting player, Nico declares first, so Albert does know Nico's declaration before choosing whether to exile their hand with Serum Powder and draw that many cards [103.5b].
- If Albert is the starting player, Albert must declare (and thus decide about Serum Powder) first, without knowing Nico's choice [103.5b].

Why: Serum Powder says "Any time you could mulligan and this card is in your hand, you may exile all the cards from your hand, then draw that many cards." Rule 103.5b explicitly covers this kind of "any time [that player] could mulligan" action: the player may do it at a time they would declare whether they will take a mulligan, this need not be the first round of mulligans, other players may already have made their mulligan declarations by then, and after performing the action the player then declares whether they will take a mulligan. So Albert isn't locked in: Albert can use Serum Powder in a later mulligan round, and using it doesn't stop Albert from also mulliganing, nor does mulliganing stop Albert from using another Serum Powder drawn later [Serum Powder ruling #1]. Note the exiled cards stay exiled for the rest of the game and are not shuffled back in on later mulligans [Serum Powder ruling #0].

This is the two-player case as asked. At a multiplayer table the same principle applies in turn order — Albert knows the declarations of every player who declared before them and none of those after; also, in multiplayer (and Brawl) a player's first mulligan doesn't count toward cards put on the bottom [103.5c], [800.6], and team games use the team-based mulligan order [805.3a].

question: Ariana controls [Sen Triplets], which targeted Nico. Nico's hand contains [Rift Sower]. Can either player suspend it? If so, who will cast it once the last time counter is removed?
answer:
Ariana can suspend Rift Sower; Nico cannot. And when the last time counter comes off, Nico — the card's owner — is the one who gets the option to cast Rift Sower without paying its mana cost.

Why Nico can't: exiling a card with suspend is a special action, and a player may take it only if they could begin to cast that card by putting it onto the stack ([116.2f], [702.62a]). Effects that prohibit casting are taken into account ([702.62c], [601.3], [Rift Sower ruling #0]). Sen Triplets says the targeted player "can't cast spells" that turn, so Nico could not begin to cast Rift Sower and therefore can't suspend it.

Why Ariana can: Sen Triplets says "You may play lands and cast spells from that player's hand this turn," so Ariana could begin to cast Rift Sower from Nico's hand and thus may take the suspend special action, paying the suspend cost of {G} and exiling Rift Sower with two time counters. Timing still follows Rift Sower's card type — Rift Sower is a creature, so this is during Ariana's main phase with an empty stack while she has priority, and Sen Triplets doesn't change when she may cast from that hand ([Sen Triplets ruling #4], [116.2f]). Note that exiling with suspend is not casting and doesn't use the stack, so it can't be responded to ([Rift Sower ruling #4]).

Who casts it later: Rift Sower is owned by Nico, and the two triggered abilities of suspend function in exile for the card's owner — counters come off at the beginning of the owner's upkeep ([702.62a], [Rift Sower ruling #1]). When the last counter is removed, the second triggered ability triggers and Nico may cast Rift Sower without paying its mana cost, ignoring normal timing permissions for its type; if Nico declines, it stays exiled and is no longer suspended ([Rift Sower ruling #5], [Rift Sower ruling #3]). Cast that way it's a creature spell, so Rift Sower gains haste ([702.62a], [Rift Sower ruling #2]).

Timing caveat: Sen Triplets' restriction lasts only "this turn." In the normal case the last counter is removed on a later turn of Nico's, so Nico can cast Rift Sower freely. If somehow the last counter were removed while Nico was still under a Sen Triplets restriction that turn, the prohibition on casting would stop Nico from casting it ([601.3]), and Rift Sower would remain exiled.

Multiplayer: Sen Triplets targets one opponent each upkeep, so this all applies only to that one targeted player (here Nico). With more than two players, other opponents are unaffected and Ariana has no permission to suspend cards from their hands. The answer is otherwise identical at two players or more.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
Wayward Angel ends up as a 1/1 blue Frog creature named Wayward Angel with no abilities (mana cost still {4}{W}{W}), for as long as Turn to Frog lasts (until end of turn).

Why:

1. While manifested, Wayward Angel was a face-down 2/2 colorless creature with no name, subtypes, or abilities — those are its characteristics and its copiable values while face down [708.2], [708.2a], [613.2b].
2. Turn to Frog resolved on that face-down object. It doesn't change copiable values; it's a continuous effect that applies in the layers: it removes all abilities, makes Wayward Angel blue, makes it a Frog, and sets base power/toughness to 1/1.
3. Turning Wayward Angel face up reverts its copiable values to its normal printed values (name Wayward Angel, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, 4/4 Angel Horror, flying, vigilance, the threshold ability), but "any effects that have been applied to the face-down permanent still apply to the face-up permanent" [708.8], [708.10]. So Turn to Frog keeps applying.
4. Turn to Frog's effect has a later timestamp than the card's own printed abilities, so its ability-removal strips flying, vigilance, and the Threshold static ability. With the Threshold ability gone, Wayward Angel does not get +3/+3, does not become black, does not gain trample, and does not gain the upkeep sacrifice trigger — even though Ariella still has seven cards in their graveyard [613.1g]. Turn to Frog also overwrites base power/toughness-setting effects, leaving base 1/1 [Turn to Frog ruling #0], and Wayward Angel loses its other colors and creature types while keeping other card types/supertypes [Turn to Frog ruling #1].
5. Turning face up doesn't trigger any "enters the battlefield" abilities [708.8]. Any counters or P/T modifiers from other sources would still apply on top of the 1/1 base [Turn to Frog ruling #2], and any ability Wayward Angel gains after Turn to Frog resolved would stick [Turn to Frog ruling #3]. Note manifest is not megamorph, so no +1/+1 counter is added on turning face up [Megamorph], [701.40h].

Timing note: I'm assuming the order you gave — Turn to Frog resolves first, then Wayward Angel is turned face up. If instead Wayward Angel were turned face up first and Turn to Frog resolved afterward, the end result this turn would be the same 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities, since Turn to Frog would still have the latest timestamp.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is identical at a two-player or multiplayer table.

answer_gold: It's a 4/4 black Frog with trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature", but no other abilities. Wayward Angel receives a new timestamp when it turns face up, so its ability is applied before Turn to Frog in each layer. Wayward Angel's last ability is removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply in layer 5 to change its color to black, it will continue doing so in later layers. Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp, so it makes Wayward Angel blue before it becomes black in layer 5 and removes Wayward Angel's abilities in layer 6 before it gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature".

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its full type line ends up as "Legendary Land Creature — Swamp Elemental" (a 6/4 green creature).

How it gets there, following the timestamp order you gave:

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth says "Each land is a Swamp in addition to its other land types," which includes Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth itself, so it gains the land type Swamp while keeping everything else about it (name, legendary supertype, abilities) [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0].
2. Kormus Bell then makes all Swamps — controlled by any player — 1/1 black creatures that are still lands, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth becomes both a land and a creature, affected by anything that affects either type [Kormus Bell ruling #0], [Kormus Bell ruling #1]. Kormus Bell grants no creature type on its own.
3. Conspiracy (naming Ferret) makes creatures you control the chosen type and they lose all their other creature types [Conspiracy ruling #4]; it can indeed grant a creature type to animated lands that would otherwise have none [Conspiracy ruling #1].
4. Vastwood Zendikon, the most recent of these effects to begin applying, makes the enchanted land a 6/4 green Elemental creature that's still a land [Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5]. Because it both sets power/toughness and sets the creature type, and it has the latest timestamp, it overwrites the earlier type-setting effects: the 1/1 black from Kormus Bell is overwritten to 6/4 green [Vastwood Zendikon ruling #0], and the creature type Elemental replaces Ferret.

So the only creature type is Elemental; Swamp is a land type, not a creature type, and it stays because Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth grants it "in addition to" other land types. The Legendary supertype is unaffected — changing card types or subtypes doesn't change supertypes [205.4b], [205.1b]. Note Conspiracy still makes your other creatures Ferrets; it just loses the type-setting race on this particular permanent.

Caveat on my grounding: the layer/timestamp rules (rule 613) were not included in the context provided to me, so the "which type-setting effect wins" step above rests on Vastwood Zendikon ruling #0's statement that a later land-animation effect overwrites the previous one. If you instead treated Conspiracy as applying after Vastwood Zendikon, the creature type would be Ferret rather than Elemental (the 6/4 green body would be unchanged either way).

Also note this is all independent of player count: Kormus Bell affects every player's Swamps, while Conspiracy only affects creatures Ahmad controls, so with more than two players nothing about Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own types changes.
